paras: The lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt was the hanging of three young Black people by a crowd of white and Black residents near Salem, Clarendon County, South Carolina, on or about December 8, 1880. The three were accused of killing Mrs. Thomas Kennedy, a young white woman, while robbing her house, and were hanged after the crowd voted against handing them to the courts. The Charleston News and Courier's account ran across the country, and South Carolina papers cited the case for months as a justified lynching.

According to a letter to the News and Courier from New Zion, Thomas Kennedy left home on Sunday, December 5, to ask his mother to stay with his wife while he visited Charleston. Returning about three hours later, he found his wife, formerly Ada Wright of Darlington, dead outside the front gate with her skull split, and the house had been plundered. An inquest returned a verdict of murder "by unknown hands."

Several Black people were arrested on Monday and released for lack of evidence. On Tuesday Joe Barnes, about 16, who was said to have worked for Kennedy the week before, was arrested and, by the correspondent's account, confessed that Vance Brandt, 18, and his sister Julia, 15, had planned a robbery and struck Mrs. Kennedy with hoes. The Brandts denied any part in it, and the case against them rested on Barnes's statement, blood on their clothes, and Kennedy's money and pistol said to have been found with them.

A crowd then gathered to decide the prisoners' fate. The Charleston wire put it at 150 white men and 50 Black men and said the Black men asked to burn the prisoners alive but were refused. A vote was taken on whether to jail the three and await the court, and "only twenty-three voted to await the law." The New Zion letter instead described a crowd of 250 to 300, "both white and colored," that decided "after due deliberation" to hang them.

The three were taken to the tree nearest the scene of the murder, in sight of the Kennedy gate. Ropes were tied to a limb, the prisoners were made to mount a cart, and their faces were covered with handkerchiefs. Barnes asked to pray, and when the cart was pushed away all three were hanged.

No report of an inquest on the three, an arrest of anyone in the crowd, or any official inquiry appears in the coverage. A year-end South Carolina chronology in the Anderson Intelligencer listed the lynching under December 8. In April 1881, defending the state against a charge of a "habit of lynching," the Pickens Sentinel named it among lynchings carried out for "heinous" crimes.

The first notice was a brief Charleston dispatch printed by the New-York Tribune on December 10. A fuller wire drawn from the News and Courier followed on December 11 and ran in New York, Chicago, Dallas, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Illinois papers between December 11 and 16. Headline writers called the three "Fiends" and the hanging "Just and Speedy Retribution," and the Centre Democrat headed its copy "Butchered by Negroes."

In South Carolina, the Abbeville Press and Banner reprinted the News and Courier letter under "The Clarendon Outrage and Its Speedy Punishment," with the deck "The Guilt Fully Proved." The Newberry Herald and the Baptist Courier stressed that whites and Black people took part in the hanging. The Orangeburg Democrat called the accused "three young colored demons" and argued that when the law was too slow, "it becomes proper and necessary to deal summarily with offenders." Every report took the confession and the crowd's examination as proof of guilt, and none questioned the hanging.

Most reports date the murder to Sunday, December 5, but the Orangeburg Democrat gives the 4th and a Wilmington Star correspondent "Monday evening." That correspondent, writing on December 8, said a mob of 100 citizens arrested "a man, a woman and a boy," while other papers described the three as two men and a woman or as two boys and a girl. A Minnesota digest dated the lynching to the 9th, but the December 8 letter already reported it.

reader.title: Lynching of Joe Barnes, Vance Brandt and Julia Brandt
bases: A crowd of white and Black residents hanged three Black people accused of murdering Mrs. Thomas Kennedy after voting not to hand them to the courts (A3, A9, A15).

Three accused people were hanged by a crowd variously put at 100, 200, or 250-300 (A3, A9, A13), which voted against jailing them to await the court (A3, A15); the pretext was punishment for the alleged murder and robbery (A9).

The News and Courier letter and wire (A3, A9), a separate Wilmington Star correspondent (A13), and South Carolina weeklies (A10, A12, A15) agree that three Black people accused of the Kennedy murder were hanged by a crowd near the scene.

accounts.label: News and Courier correspondent (New Zion, Dec. 9)
accounts.gist: Written 'at the request of many citizens, both black and white', it gives Barnes's confession as the account of the murder and says a crowd of 250-300 white and Black citizens 'after due deliberation' hanged the three near the scene.

accounts.label: Charleston wire (Dec. 11)
accounts.gist: From the same News and Courier details, it puts the crowd at 150 white and 50 Black men, says the Black men asked to burn the prisoners and were refused, and reports a vote in which only 23 favored awaiting the court.

accounts.label: Wilmington Star correspondent (Williamsburg County, Dec. 8)
accounts.gist: Dates the murder to 'Monday evening' and says a mob of 100 citizens arrested a man, a woman and a boy, who confessed and were lynched.

framing.detail: The News and Courier letter was headed 'THE CLARENDON OUTRAGE AND ITS SPEEDY PUNISHMENT' with 'The Guilt Fully Proved' and called the crowd's rage natural.
The Orangeburg Democrat called the accused 'three young colored demons' and argued that the slow processes of the law sometimes justify summary action.
Northern and western papers ran the Charleston wire under headlines such as 'A TRIPLE LYNCHING. Three Fiends Hanged' and 'Just and Speedy Retribution'.
In April 1881 the Pickens Sentinel cited the hanging to deny a 'habit of lynching weak and defenceless negroes' in South Carolina.
